entities.summary:
Notre-Dame de Paris is the most famous Gothic cathedral in the world, built between 1163 and 1345 CE on the Île de la Cité in the heart of Paris. The cathedral revolutionized Gothic architecture with its innovative flying buttresses, pioneering rose windows, and masterful synthesis of structural engineering with artistic achievement — becoming the definitive model for Gothic cathedrals across France and Europe.

Bishop Maurice de Sully began construction in 1163 on a site of previous churches, with King Louis VII attending the foundation ceremony. The early Gothic structure pioneered flying buttresses which, by transferring the thrust of the vaulted ceiling to exterior supports, allowed enormously tall, thin walls filled with stained glass rather than thick stone. The three rose windows — south (1260), north (1250), and west (1200s) — remain among the finest medieval stained glass in existence.

Notre-Dame witnessed pivotal moments in French and European history: the coronation of Henry VI of England as King of France (1431), Napoleon's coronation as Emperor (1804), Masses after French liberation (1944), and the funeral of Charles de Gaulle (1970). Victor Hugo's novel Notre-Dame de Paris (1831) — The Hunchback of Notre-Dame — sparked massive public interest in the threatened building, creating the modern historic preservation movement. The April 2019 fire that destroyed the spire and much of the roof became a global moment of grief, followed by a remarkable €840 million international restoration campaign.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Notre-Dame de Paris is the world's most recognized Gothic cathedral, a symbol of Western civilization's spiritual and artistic achievements, and through its 2019 fire and restoration, a living monument to collective human memory and cultural solidarity.
